results.title: CoreWeave struggling to keep up with demand for Nvidia chips, CEO says
highlights:
SAN FRANCISCO, Calif. — What's good for Nvidia (NVDA) looks to be good for its key partner in the AI infrastructure boom, CoreWeave (CRWV). 

"We are struggling to meet demand every day," CoreWeave CEO Michael Intrator told Yahoo Finance from the Goldman Sachs Communacopia & Tech Conference (video above). "Every GPU we have could be sold to multiple different clients. It is a unique moment, and it continues to be." 

Nvidia serves as the backbone, primary supplier, and main financial guarantor for CoreWeave's ever-expansive neocloud operation. 

Beyond supplying 100% of the advanced GPUs powering CoreWeave's specialized AI data centers, Nvidia acts as a major strategic shareholder, holding an 11.5% equity stake.

...

Nvidia said after reporting its fiscal second quarter earnings that it sees 70% revenue growth for fiscal year 2028, above analyst forecasts for 45% growth. The sales gain would be larger — think in excess of 100% — if not for memory chip shortages, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said. 

That demand outlook should keep CoreWeave's business humming. 

CoreWeave reported that second quarter sales surged 112% year over year. Adjusted operating profits more than doubled to $1.5 billion. 

Driven by explosive enterprise demand for graphics processing unit (GPU) compute and a massive $104 billion total revenue backlog, management raised its full-year 2026 revenue guidance to a range of $12.4 billion to $13.2 billion.

Each row is one GPU model. On-demand is Aven Cloud's current single-GPU rate, adjusted continuously to supply and demand; spot is the interruptible rate for the same GPU where one is listed, and it can move on every refresh. Public cloud range is the low-to-high published on-demand list price for a comparable single-GPU instance across the three largest public clouds. Savings compares Aven Cloud's on-demand price with the high end of that range — the list price most buyers actually pay before any negotiated discount — and a short sparkline shows how Aven Cloud's own on-demand price has moved over time.

For example, Aven Cloud's current on-demand rate for a single H100 SXM5 is $4.51/GPU-hour, against a public range of $6.90-$12.29 — up to 63% lower than the top of that range. A GPU with no public-cloud reference yet, because it's too new or too specialized for a clean single-GPU match, shows the Aven Cloud price on its own rather than a guessed comparison.

To put that in hours: renting a single H100 SXM5 for 24 hours costs $108.24 on Aven Cloud at the on-demand rate above — up to 63% less than the same 24 hours at the top of the public-cloud range, with no egress fees or minimum term added on top.

...

The aggregate figure at the top of the table is a simple average of the 1-GPU on-demand prices available that day — not weighted by usage, and it can move when a GPU is added to or dropped from the comparison, not only when a price changes. List prices are also not the whole story on either side: a hyperscaler customer with a negotiated enterprise discount or reserved capacity may pay less than the list price shown here, just as an Aven Cloud spot price isn't directly comparable to an on-demand list price. Treat the index as a fair, sourced starting point — not the final word on any one contract.

results.title: GPU Pricing Splits as Spot Rates Triple and Capacity Goes to Auction — TechReaderDaily
highlights:
Spot GPU rental rates tripled in Nebius Group's Q2 2026 results while a new auction market is trying to put a real number on reserved GPU capacity.

...

GPU spot rental rates tripled. That opening figure came out of Nebius Group's Q2 2026 earnings call on August 12, 2026, as reported by Morningstar. The unit is worth holding still: a spot rate is the price of a GPU-hour on a short horizon, clearing against scarcity in the moment rather than against a multi-month reservation. In an industry that publicly prices capacity in gigawatts and privately prices contracts in months, a tripled spot rate is the single number that repriced the room without anyone having to renegotiate a thing.

Five days earlier, the other side of the market started moving. On August 4, Fluence launched GPU Cluster Auctions, a marketplace for reserved GPU capacity that lets AI teams run competitive bids for clusters instead of accepting a posted term sheet. Reuters carried the announcement. Spot capacity reprices too fast. Reserved capacity reprices too slowly. An auction is the attempt to make the slow side produce a number.

> GPU spot rental rates continue to climb as the artificial intelligence supply/demand imbalance intensifies and neoclouds want to maximize value extracted from short-term pricing. Morningstar, August 12, 2026

The second clause of that sentence is the analytical center. The neoclouds were not framed as cost-passing utilities. Morningstar used the word maximize. For a buyer, that changes the negotiating position. The seller is a market maker monetizing a supply gap, not a capacity landlord collecting a fixed margin. The behavior matches the pricing: short-term scarcity is the product, and the spot book is where it gets marked to market.

The retail channel shows the same appetite in raw dollars. Gaming GPU prices rose as much as 41 percent between June and August 2026, according to MSN, and the sellers did not suffer. PC Partner Group, the Hong Kong-listed parent of Zotac, Inno3D, and Manli, reported on August 14 that its net profit doubled. TechSpot tracked prices across 10 countries and found GeForce cards taking the biggest hit. The margin did not leak to discounters; it stayed in the vendor ledger.

Geography does not soften the move. MSN reported on August 5 that RTX 50 GPU prices surged as much as 50 percent in South Korea, the country where Samsung and SK Hynix produce the GDDR7 memory in every card in that series. A memory maker's home market paying a 50 percent premium is not a freight story. It is an upstream constraint priced through the local shelf, and it confirms the shortage has no insulated zone.

The entry tier shows the same constraint moving sideways. TechSpot reported on August 17 that PC Partner Group expects lower-priced graphics cards to tighten further in the second half of 2026 as memory costs push prices up and limit supply. That is a second-order effect with a first-order cause: AI accelerator demand is drawing memory away from budget cards. The notebook and entry desktop buyer is now the residual bidder in the same queue as inference capacity.

The margin question has different answers in different markets. In retail, PC Partner booked a doubling profit while buyers absorbed 41 percent and 50 percent moves. In cloud, Morningstar's note frames the neocloud as the party that maximizes value from short-term price spikes. The chip, the card vendor, and the cloud operator all captured a slice. The team renting by the hour gets the invoice. That is the recurring pattern of this cycle: the bottleneck earns, the tenant pays.

...

A GPU-hour is not a token price. The distinction is the gap most buyers miss. A rented accelerator bills by the hour whether the tenant runs at batch size 32 or batch size 1, but the token count produced inside that hour changes with batching, sequence length, and utilization. A tripled spot rate in dollars per GPU-hour does not imply a tripled cost per token. It implies whatever throughput assumptions the buyer brings to the invoice. Shoppers who compare only hourly rates are pricing air.

...

The procurement menu now shows three prices. Spot rental rates tripled in Nebius's Q2 call. Reserved capacity is moving toward auction clearing. Retail cards stood 40 percent above their old street prices on Newegg over the summer, per PCGamesN, and the entry tier is expected to tighten again. A team that anchors to any one of those numbers is running a single-source pricing model in a market that has stopped behaving like one.

...

Allocation follows the same logic. Inference with a defined floor belongs on reserved capacity; burst traffic belongs on spot. But Nebius's numbers show spot rising fastest, which inverts the historical relationship. Spot used to be the cheap overflow valve, priced below the committed tier because it was residual supply. When spot triples while reserved goes to auction, the overflow valve starts billing like a premium service, and the allocation decision becomes a hedge rather than a routing rule.

results.title: H100 Rents Give Back Nvidia's 22% Bounce
highlights:
Nvidia founder and CEO Jensen Huang on September 8 amplified a chart showing H100 rentals at $3.28 an hour, up 22% in a month. The same Ornn index’s settled H100 print of $2.92 on September 24 was down 1.8% over 30 days from $2.97.

That 17-day drop from $3.28 to $2.92 is 11%, and it landed while Nvidia still posted $96.2 billion quarterly revenue and a market value near $5.41 trillion. A noisy neocloud tape is a thin way to close a fight about how Big Tech books GPU lives.

...

The settled daily series on Ornn’s public page never treated that $3.28 hour as a durable level. By September 24 the index was $2.92 per GPU-hour, or $70.02 per GPU-day and about $2,100.60 per GPU-month, after a 4.3% one-day drop from $3.05. The seven-day change was still +2.4%. The 30-day change was not.

...

OCPI-H100 is not a hyperscaler list price and not a used-chip bid. Ornn Data LLC publishes it as a settlement-style benchmark of on-demand H100 SXM rentals, listed on Bloomberg and built as a volume-weighted winsorized mean of executed trades over a rolling one-hour window, then settled once a trading day at 4:00 p.m. ET.

...

The rental tape already prices that ladder. On September 24, Ornn’s settled prints were $2.92 for H100 SXM, $5.16 for H200, $8.01 for B200, and $1.02 for A100 SXM4. An H100 hour cleared at 36% of a B200 hour, or about 2.7 times cheaper on a raw GPU-hour, before anyone adjusts for tokens per watt.

results.title: H100 Rental Prices Surge 22%: Why Can NVIDIA (NVDA) Older Chips Still Raise Prices, and Have AI Compute "Moats" Been Undervalued? | Gate Blog
highlights:
The chip released three years ago saw its rental price rise 22% within a single month. This unusual move allowed NVIDIA (NVDA.US) CEO Jensen Huang to address—on social media—questions about AI hardware depreciation. On September 7 local time, Huang reshared an index chart from compute marketplace Ornn. The chart showed that the on-demand rental price for NVIDIA H100 training chips had climbed to $3.28 per hour, up about 22% from the previous month. Source: X/@JensenHuang

...

At the data level, the H100’s rental price is not just starting to rebound. Ornn’s index shows that the settlement price on September 7 was $3.17 per hour, then rose to $3.28. A month earlier, the price was about $2.69 per hour, implying a roughly 22% increase over the month.

The primary factor behind this price movement is a supply-demand imbalance. Today, NVIDIA’s latest Blackwell system is still in the early stage of capacity ramp-up. With limited supply, orders from top-tier customers get prioritized, and ordinary tenants have difficulty securing access to next-generation compute resources. Against this backdrop, a large share of inference workloads can only keep running on legacy clusters such as H100. Meanwhile, power capacity and memory bandwidth at data centers remain constrained, pushing up the price floor across the entire compute rental market.

Another factor that cannot be ignored is ongoing expansion of downstream demand. Estimates suggest that the ratio of future inference compute demand to training compute demand will reach more than 3 to 1. That means compute has shifted from being a phase-based investment to an ongoing operating cost. In Q2 2026, the year-over-year revenue growth rates related to AI for three major overseas cloud providers all exceeded 37%. NVIDIA’s data center business in that quarter achieved revenue of $89 billion, up 117% year over year. When new cards are in short supply and demand remains in a fast-growth mode, legacy chip rental prices can receive support—and even rebound—making the logic internally consistent.

...

The most concerning factor in this rent increase comes from the industry-chain financing side. Cloud service providers represented by CoreWeave have been buying NVIDIA chips with large-scale debt and renting them out to external customers. By the end of June 2026, CoreWeave’s liabilities reached $35 billion. Its debt-to-equity ratio exceeded 800%, and its working capital shortfall was more than $10 billion.

More importantly, NVIDIA has "leaseback" arrangements with these partners. NVIDIA agrees to lease back unused capacity from its partner network. In effect, it provides a backstop for downstream demand. Critics argue that this off-balance-sheet arrangement may artificially inflate real compute demand, distorting the rental price signals.

...

With H100 rental prices up 22% in one month, this data in the short term reflects the real compute supply-and-demand landscape—and it is also a strong argument for Jensen Huang’s response to depreciation concerns. However, it is not a single determining metric for the long-term value of NVDA stock.

Behind this price surge, there is solid support from a structural spike in inference demand and a supply bottleneck for new cards. There are also human factors amplified by leverage across the industry chain. If rental prices hold steady or continue rising over the coming months, the market will likely reprice the economic life of NVIDIA chips—providing a positive support to NVDA’s valuation logic. But if the rental rebound is proven to be only a short-term supply disruption layered with off-balance-sheet "manufactured" demand, and the repayment stress of highly leveraged tenants is the first to blow up, then the current valuation framework built on the "compute is perpetually scarce" assumption will face a stress test.

results.title: H100 GPU Rental Rates Climb to $3.28/hr in 2026 Despite Chip Age · The Information Machine
highlights:
The gist

H100 rental prices rising through 2026 despite the chip being three years old and a successor generation shipping signals that AI inference demand is outpacing available compute supply. The projected decline toward $1/hr by mid-2027 will affect cost planning for anyone budgeting AI inference infrastructure.

...

The full picture

H100 one-year contract rental rates rose roughly 40% between October 2025 ($1.70/hr) and July 2026 (~$2.80/hr), with spot prices reaching $3.28/hr in September 2026 per the Ornn index. Marketplace median rates sit at $3.38/hr, with the cheapest tracked rate at $1.49/hr on Vast.ai. The price increase occurred even after Nvidia's Blackwell generation shipped, contrary to standard hardware depreciation patterns. The primary demand driver is AI inference for reasoning and agentic workloads, which consume far more tokens per request than simple chat. Supply constraints include TSMC CoWoS packaging capacity, HBM memory output, and 36-52 week lead times against a roughly 3.6 million unit industry backlog; HBM costs rose around 30% in Q4 2025. AWS raised H200 instance prices 15% in January 2026. Newer chips command higher rates: the H200 runs $3.59-$4.59/hr, the B200 $5.63-$8.64/hr, while AMD MI300X undercuts Nvidia equivalents at as low as $1.85/hr on Vultr. H100 rates are projected to drift toward $1/hr by mid-2027 as B200 absorbs premium demand, following the depreciation curve the A100 followed.

results.title: Nvidia's Rentable GPU Thesis: What the Data Actually Shows
highlights:
- Rising H100 rental prices reflect supply shortages, not inherent durability, as older GPUs fill gaps while Blackwell chips face 3-7 month lead times.

- CoreWeave's 9-year A100 contract shows older GPUs retain value in legacy data centers, but power infrastructure constraints—not silicon longevity—drive this.

...

On September 8, Nvidia NVDA-- CEO Jensen Huang replied to a social media post with four words that read like a finance pitch: "NVIDIA compute is fungible, durable and highly rentable." He was responding to data from Ornn Exchange showing H100 rental prices rose 22% to $3.28 per hour. For hardware that should be depreciating, the number seemed to prove his broader thesis: AI chips behave like revenue-generating infrastructure, not like equipment that steadily loses value.

...

The rental data Huang cited is real, but it doesn't prove what he's implying. Rising H100 rental prices in September 2026 don't demonstrate that GPUs are durable infrastructure. They demonstrate something more mundane: there isn't enough of the newer stuff to go around. Nvidia's Blackwell GPUs (B200, GB200) have been in limited supply, with lead times stretching to three to seven months through early 2026. When the frontier chips are backordered, older generation hardware fills the gap — and the gap pays.

The stronger evidence for Huang's durability thesis comes from an unexpected source. CoreWeave, the GPU rental specialist, signed a customer contract for Nvidia A100 GPUs running through 2029. The A100 shipped in May 2020. That's a nine-year revenue stream from a single piece of silicon. CoreWeave CEO Mike Intrator told investors that older-generation pricing is "at or above where it was years ago," and that H100s from an expired contract were immediately rebooked at 95% of their original price. Nvidia CFO Colette Kress separately noted that A100s sold six years ago still run at full utilization.

...

Old Nvidia GPUs don't last because the silicon is durable. They last because the power infrastructure is locked in.

An air-cooled DGX A100 rack draws roughly 6.5 kilowatts at full load. It fits into legacy data center halls built for about 20 kilowatts per rack. Nvidia's current Blackwell systems — the GB200 and GB300 NVL72 racks — require 120 to 140 kilowatts and direct-to-chip liquid cooling. A legacy hall can't take a Blackwell rack without a complete rebuild of power delivery and cooling infrastructure. So the A100 stays. Not because it's fast enough for frontier training, but because it's the only thing that fits in the buildings that are already built, already energized, and already paid for.

...

But there's a third variable neither Huang nor the bears fully address. The rental price evidence Huang cited comes from a market that's currently constrained by supply. H100 rental prices are rising because demand outstrips available capacity, not because a three-year-old chip is a structurally superior asset. The entire rental economics argument is inverted if supply catches up with demand — which it's headed to do. Four of the largest hyperscalers plan a combined $630 billion in capital expenditures for 2026, a 62% increase from 2025. If that capacity comes online, the scarcity premium evaporates.

Nvidia's chips are rentable today because they're scarce and because the power grid can't upgrade fast enough. Neither condition is permanent.

results.title: Flopper Now Tracks GPU Rental Prices Across 24 Cloud Providers | Flopper.io
highlights:
337 per-GPU hourly rates from 24 clouds, refreshed every six hours, with price history back to July 2026. The spec database now tells you what each accelerator costs to rent, and who is cheapest today.

...

Flopper.io started as a specification database: peak TFLOPS by precision, memory, bandwidth and power for every datacenter GPU. Specs answer half of the buying question. The other half is price, and that number lives on 24 different pricing pages, in 24 different units. As of today, the pricing index collects 337 live listings from 24 GPU cloud providers, covering 89 GPUs, normalized to one unit: US dollars per GPU per hour. The pipeline refreshes every six hours and has recorded every price change since 14 July 2026, so each GPU page now carries a price history alongside its spec sheet.

## What the Same GPU Costs, Cloud to Cloud

The spread is the story. On the day of publication, an on-demand H100 SXM5 80 GB (2022) is listed by 16 providers, and the most expensive listing costs nearly seven times the cheapest. The B200 (2024) shows the same pattern with a three-fold gap across eight clouds. Some of that gap is real: interconnect, storage, support and region all cost money. Some of it is simply price discovery that has not happened yet, because nobody was lining the numbers up.

| GPU | Providers | Cheapest on-demand | Highest on-demand |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| NVIDIA H100 SXM5 80 GB | 16 | $1.79/hr | $12.29/hr |
| NVIDIA A100 SXM4 80 GB | 11 | $1.40/hr | $4.10/hr |
| NVIDIA L40S 48 GB | 11 | $0.87/hr | $2.25/hr |
| NVIDIA H200 SXM 141 GB | 10 | $2.99/hr | $10.60/hr |
| NVIDIA B200 SXM 180 GB | 8 | $4.09/hr | $14.00/hr |
| NVIDIA B300 SXM 288 GB | 6 | $7.40/hr | $11.19/hr |
| AMD Instinct MI300X 192 GB | 5 | $2.39/hr | $6.00/hr |

On-demand, per-GPU, USD, as recorded on 9 September 2026. Spot, community and reserved listings are excluded from the range. Each GPU links to its live pricing page, which will have moved on by the time you read this.

...

A price comparison that only shows today cannot tell you whether $2.99 for an H200 is a bargain or the new ... Since 14 July 2026 the pipeline has recorded 2,297 price points across 58 days and 101 GPUs, appending a row every time a listing changes. Each GPU pricing page plots the last 30 days with one line per provider, so you can see who cut, who held, and who quietly raised.

...

## What It Does Not Cover Yet

Public list prices only. Negotiated enterprise rates, reserved-capacity contracts and volume discounts are not published and are not tracked. Availability is shown where a provider publishes it, and a listed price does not guarantee capacity in the region you need. AWS and Google Cloud are the largest gaps in coverage; both publish pricing in formats that need heavier parsing and validation, and both are next on the list.

Confirm the live rate with the provider before committing. Some outbound links are affiliate links, which fund the pipeline and never change which provider appears cheapest.
